newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles fight last battles of long flood ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Poles fight last battles of long flood ordeal.

text.p: Anthony Barker
Poles fought the last desperate battles of their three-week flood disaster on Friday as high-water surges on the Odra (Oder) river strained weakened dikes.
"Our worst problem is maintaining the anti-flood dikes. They are as soaked as a sponge," national crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes told Reuters in Warsaw.
One high-water swell, having spared the city of Opole from a repeat of earlier heavy flooding, was due to reach the city of Wroclaw late in the day.
Wroclaw spokesman Aleksander Wozny said the swell, caused by rains last weekend over heavily flooded west and south Poland, was lower than at first feared.

He said no repeat of the inundation that turned Wroclaw city centre streets into raging torrents two weeks ago was now expected, but the surge threatened outlying settlements that were home to tens of thousands of people.
Along the Odra and several other rivers, tens of thousands of troops and volunteers shored up sandbag walls and waited to pounce on any signs of weakness in defences.

The swell approaching Wroclaw was a lesser repeat of a rush of water earlier in July when floods inundated 6,000 sq km of Poland, struck more than 1,200 towns and villages and killed at least 55 people.

High water was still wreaking havoc elsewhere on the Odra, especially along the German border, where a second dike burst overnight south of the German city of Frankfurt an der Oder, prompting the evacuation of thousands from nearby villages.
So massive was the flow into the German countryside that it eased the pressure further north on the river, officials said.
Poland's Meteorology and Water Economy Institute said scattered rain and thunderstorms were expected over Poland at the weekend and Monday, but not enough to renew the floods.
Hundreds of towns and villages were still partly flooded, and dozens were completely under water in the southwest.
The fervently awaited retreat of the waters was set to usher in a host of new problems.
For victims returning to shattered homes or drowned livestock, there was the challenge of cleaning up and avoiding the dysentery and other illness threatened by the universal filth.
The government also faced serious political and economic challenges as it mobilised a vast relief and reconstruction effort estimated in billions of dollars.

The ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance's (SLD) smaller coalition partner, the Peasant party, was deciding whether to back opposition calls for a general election due on September 21 to be delayed because of the flooding.
The ex-communists, citing a need to show Poland's democratic stability, insisted they be held on time.
The SLD, accused by the opposition and media of delay and bungling, got a boost from the first opinion poll to be conducted since the floods.

Private Radio Zet said the poll, run in July 10-20 by the public CBOS institute, gave the SLD 26 percent support ahead of its biggest challenger, the Solidarity union-led AWS opposition alliance, with 22 percent.
But a CBOS sociologist said most of the polling was carried out before the public was fully aware of the scope of the disaster or the full controversy around initial relief efforts.
Some economists warned that the flood and the effects of government relief efforts could aggravate economic problems associated with Poland's budget and current account deficits.
But the zloty currency, defended from speculative selling by central bank intervention on Thursday, rose on the foreign exchange market.
